The critique's point about the Kalshi 'first Democrat to announce' market (22-27%) is not a true divergence: that market is about ordering, not timing, and most first-mover announcements in an open cycle historically land in spring/summer 2027, not December 2026. I give modest weight to the critique's fatter-tail argument (open-cycle base rates skew ~15%, 'fate will determine that' implies reactivity), but this is offset by time decay — no announcement has materialized through mid-2026 — so I settle marginally below the 12.5% Polymarket anchor at 10%.

The identical-question Polymarket anchor sits at 13% with a stable 9.5-18% range and a mild downward 30-day drift, and independent base-rate modeling of open-seat announcement timing (~4-9%) converges near the same place. Newsom has repeatedly and explicitly deferred any decision to after the November 2026 midterms, and his governorship runs to Jan 4, 2027, leaving only a ~7-week window for a declaration that would break his own stated timeline. The critique is right that advisor denials are boilerplate and that post-midterm December announcements have real precedent (Castro Dec 2018, Warren's Dec 31, 2018 exploratory committee), plus the DOJ probe and the 23-28% 'first Democrat to announce' market argue for not going far below consensus — so I nudge up slightly rather than settling at 9%. Balancing these, I land just below the market anchor at ~11.5% Yes, since the strongest structural facts (sitting governor through Jan 4, explicit post-midterm framing, no exploratory committee or early-state hires as of Aug 2026) all point to a 2027 announcement.

Major meteor strike (10kt+) in 2026?.rationale: Both forecasters and the sub-question decomposition agree: no ≥10kt event through mid-September 2026, largest event ~1.1kt, and a Poisson remaining-year estimate of ~6–8% that aligns with the 9% Polymarket anchor and coherent sibling threshold markets (5kt≈24%, 1Mt≈1.5%). The critique raises valid points about small-N uncertainty in λ and unlisted DoD detections, but these mostly widen uncertainty symmetrically rather than shift the central estimate; a genuine ≥10kt airburst would almost certainly have surfaced in fireball/news coverage even if CNEOS listing lagged. The record AMS fireball count reflects sighting/reporting growth, not large-body flux, so it adds negligible tail risk. I land between the forecasters' 8% and the market's 9%, slightly favoring the market given the acknowledged λ uncertainty and possible upward revisions.

Both forecasters correctly time-condition the Poisson base rate: with no ≥10kt event through ~August, only ~4 months of exposure remain, giving a memoryless forward probability of roughly 4-6% (1−e^(−λ/3) at λ=0.11–0.19). The critique's strongest point is the unexplained 2x gap to the rising Polymarket anchor (14.5%), which may reflect informed positioning on classified-sensor reporting lag or an unverified proxy — this warrants slightly more weight to Yes than the 7-8% consensus, but not full anchor adoption since the market plausibly hasn't fully time-decayed and full-year base rates cap at ~17% pre-conditioning. The AMS attribution of the Q1 fireball uptick to detection changes, and all 2026 events being an order of magnitude below threshold, support No. I set Yes at 9%, modestly above consensus to account for the anchor gap, contested historical count (N=4-7), and late-report optionality.

With ~7.5 of 12 months of 2026 elapsed and no confirmed ≥10kt CNEOS/IAWN event, only the remaining ~37.5% of the year is at risk: at plausible λ of 0.25–0.50/yr this gives 9–17% remaining-year probability, centering near 12%. The critique is fair that Forecast 1 anchors too tightly to the low-λ end while ignoring both detection-improvement upside and the CNEOS classification-lag channel (an already-occurred but unlogged 2026 event), so I nudge slightly above the midpoint of the two forecasts. The Polymarket proxy at 15% and rising is an imperfect anchor with modest volume and typical longshot premium, but its upward drift despite elapsing zero-event months argues against going much below 10%. Net: ~11.5% Yes, just under the proxy price and consistent with elapsed-time-discounted Poisson math across a range of λ assumptions.

Will the highest score achieved on Human.rationale: The official leaderboard sits at 46.44%, requiring a steep +13.5-point gain in ~4 months on a benchmark explicitly designed to resist saturation, with the growth trajectory visibly decelerating. The critique correctly flags that both forecasts under-weighted the verification-lag mechanism (unofficial 55-65% scores are entirely self-reported, 0 verified) and the direct base-rate analog of analysts' failed '50% by end-2025' prediction, plus the thin, momentum-driven Polymarket proxy price deserves heavier discounting. However, frontier capability does appear near the threshold per multiple third-party trackers, and a single verified Q4 frontier release could clear 60% given historical 10-15pt jumps per release cycle. I pull below both forecasts toward the logistic-fit midpoint, landing at 60% YES — meaningfully below the 73.5% market anchor but respecting the genuine upside from continued rapid iteration.

The resolution-relevant official CAIS/Scale leaderboard sits at ~46.4% as of Aug 2026, requiring ~14 points in four months — above the trailing pace and well above the early-2026 deceleration of ~1.3 pts/mo — which is the strongest case for No. However, the official site is demonstrably lagging rather than capping: independent no-tools trackers already report 55–56% (Fable 5, Opus 5), so a single official refresh plus one more frontier launch (GPT-6/Gemini 4-class/Deep Think update) could clear 60% without any re-acceleration in true capability. The 72.5% Polymarket anchor deserves discounting because it is only a proxy for the actual ticker, may resolve on looser 'any reported score' wording, and moved on tool-assisted BenchLM headlines whose methodology (and self-reported-benchmark CoI concerns) is disputed. Weighing the critique's points on resolution ambiguity, institutional update cadence, and the Monte Carlo's wider/lower 45–55% band, I settle modestly below both the market and Forecast 1 but above the conservative scenario: 65% Yes.

Resolution hinges solely on the official agi.safe.ai/Scale CAIS no-tools leaderboard, which sits at ~37.5–46.4% — a required jump of ~14–23 points in roughly the final four months of 2026, larger in absolute terms than any prior comparable window and against a visibly decelerating official curve. The 55–65% figures from BenchLM/Artificial Analysis are the main Yes pathway but are unverified, plausibly tool-augmented or ensemble-based, and in one case (Muse Spark 1.1) actively disputed for conflict of interest; a contested posting adds two-sided tail risk rather than clean upside. Label-noise (~30% flawed chem/bio items) imposes a genuine ceiling, though an 'HLE-Verified' revision that strips unanswerable questions is an underappreciated mechanical route to a Yes. I weight the trajectory-based Monte Carlo (35–40%) more heavily than the thin, volatile $18K Polymarket quote (56%, range 45–71.5%), landing modestly below both prior forecasts at 40% Yes.

Clarity Act (H.R.3633) signed into law i.rationale: Both forecasters and both prediction markets (Polymarket ~27.5%, Kalshi <25%) converge on roughly a one-in-four chance, and the brief contains no information beyond what the market has priced. The critique's concerns pull in opposite directions: a bottom-up chain (cloture with only 2 confirmed Democrats vs. 7+ needed → Senate floor passage → House concurrence or conference → signature in a compressed midterm/lame-duck calendar) argues for a somewhat lower number, while the sharp +13pt Polymarket move into the 9/15 cloture vote, active Trump/Bessent/Armstrong lobbying, and the GENIUS Act precedent argue that a live path exists. Since the pivotal cloture outcome is unconfirmed, the appropriate stance is to stay near the well-informed market consensus rather than lean either way. I settle at 26% YES, nudged marginally toward the higher-volume Polymarket read.

Both forecasters landed near the Polymarket anchor (16.5%) and the secondary Kalshi report (<25%), and the critique, while raising valid points about compounding stage risks and lame-duck dynamics, does not identify a directional flaw that would justify moving materially away from that anchor. The sub-questions uniformly point to 'No': cloture on the motion to proceed is unsecured with only two Democrats having supported the committee bill, three substantive disputes remain open, and even Senate passage would require reconciliation with House text and Senate Agriculture's parallel bill in a midterm-year calendar. The multi-stage sequencing (cloture, floor passage, conference, House re-vote, signature) compounds against Yes, but a lame-duck session driven by Trump/industry pressure and a possible Gallego ethics deal preserves a real tail, consistent with the GENIUS Act showing crypto legislation can move under this trifecta. I settle at 16% Yes, essentially the market consensus, since the brief offers no information beyond what traders have priced.

Both forecasts converge at 14%, closely tracking the strongest available anchor (Polymarket 13.5%, secondary Kalshi ~18%). The critique raises valid points on both sides — potential upside from cloture success, must-pass vehicle riders, and GENIUS Act precedent; potential downside from the underweighted conference/reconciliation gate requiring the Senate's distinct substitute to be merged with House text, re-passed, and signed all within a post-recess ~3-month window. The market's implied conditional structure (22% cloture success × ~60% conditional completion ≈ 13.5%) is internally coherent and reflects the multi-stage decomposition the critique demands, so no shared flaw is exposed. The repeated pattern of slipped deadlines and unresolved ethics/Trump-conflict disputes justifies staying at or slightly below the anchor rather than above it. Final: 13% Yes.

The binding constraint is vote arithmetic: Republicans have ~51 usable votes and need ~9 Democratic crossovers, with zero confirmed and unresolved objections on Trump-family crypto conflicts, DeFi classification, stablecoin yield, and AML — the 9/15 cloture vote only opens debate. Both forecasters landed at 16-18%, consistent with the base-rate model (~13%) and specialist odds (Galaxy ~10%, XO ~19.5%), all well below Polymarket's 24.5%. The critique fairly notes that Polymarket's +5% post-cloture-filing bounce may embed whip-count information and that the outcome is bimodal (cloture success would sharply re-rate upward), so I nudge slightly toward the market rather than the pure base rate. Offsetting that, the critique's point about post-cloture time sinks — floor amendments, House concurrence on an amended H.R.3633, and a compressed ~14-day pre-midterm window plus a lame-duck sprint — argues that even conditional on cloture, signature by 12/31 is far from assured. Settling at 18% Yes, between the base-rate model and the Polymarket anchor.

Decomposing the sequence: P(cloture clears on/after Sept 15) ~45-50%, P(Senate final passage | cloture) ~85%, P(House concurrence with a substantially rewritten Senate substitute plus signature before Dec 31) ~60-70% given midterm-year floor scarcity and competing appropriations/NDAA business — multiplying gives roughly 0.22-0.28 gross, but the ping-pong tail (Senate passes, House re-concurrence slips past Dec 31) and the still-declining market trend pull this down. The Polymarket proxy at 18.5% is thin and volatile, so I treat it as a soft signal rather than a hard anchor, and note it converges with Galaxy's 30%-and-falling estimate and the ~25-38% historical reference class discounted for midterm calendar friction. The GENIUS Act recovery precedent is real but consumed weeks; with only ~3.5 months of session time remaining after Sept 15, that precedent actually tightens rather than widens the path. I land slightly below the proxy at 17% YES, reflecting the multiple sequential 60-vote and concurrence hurdles and unresolved ethics/DeFi/CFTC disputes with only two committee-level Democratic supporters against roughly ten needed.

The primary market anchor (Polymarket, 24.5% and eroding on a -15pt/30d trend) and the base-rate model (~12-15% for contested, House-passed, election-year bills) bracket the answer, and I land modestly below the market because the specific news flow is directionally negative: missed pre-recess window, Thune's explicit deprioritization behind nominations/NDAA/Russia sanctions, unresolved Banking/Agriculture reconciliation, and the unresolved stablecoin-yield fight. The binding constraint is cloture math — moving from 2 committee-crossover Democrats to 7+ floor votes while Murphy, Van Hollen and Merkley formally oppose the merged draft is a large swing to complete in a compressed Sept–Dec calendar, even with the ethics compromise designed to court Gillibrand and others. The critique's fair points — Trump's personal lobbying, ready merged text on Calendar No. 423, procedural progress beyond anything FIT21 achieved, and a plausible lame-duck/must-pass vehicle attachment — justify keeping YES meaningfully above the pure base rate rather than shading toward 8-12%. Netting these, ~19% for Yes reflects both the genuine live pathway and the heavy procedural/vote-math burden remaining.

Will Russia enter Dobropillia by Decembe.rationale: Mean of 5 draws (0.86, 0.87, 0.88, 0.89, 0.88). The same-question Polymarket market sits at 90% YES with a steep upward trend, and sibling deadline markets (Sep 15→Dec 31: 4%→37%→70%→90%) show strong consensus that entry is near-term. Pokrovsk and Myrnohrad have fallen, secondary reporting (CNN 9/8, Euromaidan Press 9/15) places intensified Russian infiltration at Dobropillia's immediate eastern approaches, ceasefire odds are low (~21%), and ISW's shading practice for infiltration/advance areas is relatively liberal, while the resolution criterion only requires any part of the city to be shaded. I shade slightly below the anchor because the primary ISW/DeepState shading status is unconfirmed, the 2025 Dobropillia salient was fully reversed, the 'inside the city' claims come from low-reliability sources, and the one-cycle persistence requirement could push confirmation past Dec 31 if the advance stalls at the outskirts.

The resolution bar is relatively low — any ISW shading inside city limits persisting one update cycle — and Russia is fighting at the outskirts with saturation drone strikes, renewed July momentum (+34.7 sq km), and 4.5 months remaining on its priority axis, which supports the high Polymarket anchor (85%). However, the critique correctly notes the anchor is a thin, volatile market ($97.5k volume, 34–89% range) with no Kalshi confirmation, and that both forecasters underweighted the persistence criterion given this exact axis's history of full reversals (2025 salient, June 2026 losses) and Ukraine's active dissection of the current push. The unverified outskirt-entry rumor deserves near-zero evidentiary weight since ISW explicitly reports no confirmed advance as of Aug 3. Balancing the market signal against the Monte Carlo range (57–75%) and the reversal/persistence risks, I settle near the dissenting forecast at 76% YES rather than deferring to the illiquid market price.

The resolution bar is low — ISW/DeepState shading of *any* part of Dobropillia persisting one update cycle — and Russian forces are already reported dug in on the eastern outskirts (Nove Shakhove) with approach roads cut, leaving ~4.5 months of runway. The Polymarket proxy at 88% with strong upward momentum, no ceasefire signals (talks suspended since Feb 2026; HUR expects continued offensive), and Pokrovsk/Myrnohrad's fall freeing effort for this axis all reinforce Yes. The devil's advocate correctly flags the 2025 salient reversal and the >50% weekly pace slowdown, but those cut against *capture/holding the city*, not against a brief ISW-shaded incursion into its edge, which is mechanically easier; the critique's point 6 offsets points 2–3. Residual No mass (~12%) covers resolution-criteria mismatch with the Kalshi ticker, a stalled/reversed front as in 2025, and low-probability truce scenarios. I land essentially at the market anchor.

The identical Polymarket contract at 82% YES is the only direct consensus anchor and deserves substantial weight, especially since the resolution bar is low (ISW-shaded entry into any part of the city, not capture) and Russian forces are already fighting on the immediate approaches (Nove Shakhove, Vodyane, Krasnoyarsk, claimed breach of the southern outer defensive line) with ~4.5 months remaining and no durable ceasefire. However, the red team is right that the market may be overweighting milblogger-sourced momentum on thin volume ($77.6K, +27% in 30 days), and that the persistence-through-a-full-update-cycle requirement plus the fully reversed 2025 offensive on this exact axis are meaningful discounts. The fundamentals — Russia's gain rate collapsing to ~8% of 2024-25 pace (~13 sq mi/30 days), failure to leverage Pokrovsk into follow-on advances, and the year-plus grind Pokrovsk itself required — argue for pricing well below the market, while the crude Monte Carlo's 0–30% range assumes an unverified 5–20 km gap that likely overstates the distance given fighting is reported on the outskirts. A stalled-talks freeze before Dec 31 is a low-probability but real additional route to No. I settle at 70% Yes, between the two forecasts and materially below the 82% proxy.

Will Russia enter Mykolaivka by Septembe.rationale: Both forecasters landed within a few points of the Polymarket anchor (44.5%), and the critique's arguments cut in opposite directions: the D≈0 Monte Carlo case argues for higher, while the ~16-day window, the higher full-cycle ISW shading bar, the location-conflation risk, and Ukraine's nearby Lyman counteroffensive argue for lower. The most informative signal is that despite six-plus weeks of 'fighting inside Mykolaivka' reporting, the market has not resolved and its price fell 16pp in a week — indicating qualifying ISW shading has not locked in and traders see momentum shifting toward Ukraine on this axis. Still, Russian forces are genuinely engaged at or inside the town's edge with no ceasefire prospect, so an ISW infiltration/advance marking persisting through a cycle before Sept 30 remains a substantial possibility. I settle marginally below the anchor at 43% Yes, close to the consensus, with No modestly favored.

The only available market anchor is Polymarket at 68% YES, and both forecasters pushed above it based on the Aug 23 ISW-assessed infiltration into Mykolaivka's outskirts and Sept 1-2 geolocated footage of Russians inside the settlement. The red-team correctly notes that the market fell 11.5% over the week that included this footage, and that 'clearing operations' with captured Russians is consistent with a repelled infiltration rather than persistent presence — so the bullish evidence is weaker than it first appears, and ISW's demonstrated conservatism (disputing MoD breakthrough claims, only ~90 sq km confirmed in August) means qualifying shading could lag past Sept 30. Still, Russia is actively prioritizing this axis, the town is ~10 km from the active combat cluster, ISW has already assessed infiltration there, the partial ceasefire did not freeze fighting, and ~3.5 weeks remain, which is ample for ISW's typically liberal infiltration shading to appear and persist. I land essentially at the market with a slight upward tilt, splitting the difference between the anchor and the forecasters rather than following them to 0.78.

Russian forces were reported infiltrating Mykolaivka's outskirts as of Aug 23 via ISW-affiliated Critical Threats reporting, which strongly suggests ISW's own map shading (the resolution trigger) is imminent or already present, and the bar is only shaded infiltration—not full capture—as the critique correctly notes (point 4). With ~5 weeks of runway, no ceasefire, sustained offensive momentum since Siversk's fall, and active interdiction strikes on the settlement, YES is favored above the Polymarket 66.5% anchor. However, the critique's points on the ISW shading/persistence requirement, the Aug 27 Ukrainian reinforcement, and the market's recent 18pp pullback justify keeping meaningful NO probability rather than pushing toward 0.80+. Landing at 0.73, consistent with both forecasters and modestly above the market anchor, reflects the leading-indicator strength of ISW-linked infiltration reporting balanced against confirmation lag and stabilization risk.

Multiple independent reports (euobserver Aug 19, malcontentnews Aug 21) place Russian assault/sabotage groups inside Mykolaivka's eastern edge, with Kostiantynivka effectively fallen on Aug 20 and the axis accelerating; the contract explicitly counts ISW's liberal 'Assessed Russian Infiltration Areas' layer, which historically appears within days of press-confirmed infiltration. The critique's strongest point is the resolution-mechanics gap — press infiltration is not identical to ISW shading persisting through a cycle — plus the tail case where Ukraine clears temporary recon probes; that justifies not going above ~94%, but with over five weeks of runway and repeated re-infiltration typical in Donbas urban fights, the required event needs only one qualifying map cycle, not town capture. Bakhmut/Avdiivka analogies address time-to-capture, not time-to-first-shading, so they do not much depress this specific criterion. Polymarket's 90% is thin ($15k volume) and thus only weakly informative, but it points the same direction as the underlying reporting, so I settle marginally above it at 93%.

Will ByteDance be added to the Chinese M.rationale: Mean of 5 draws (0.10, 0.10, 0.17, 0.17, 0.15). (0) Not met. The DoD/DoW release of the June 8, 2026 list (188 entities) does not show ByteDance, and every law-firm and press summary of the additions omits it. No source shows ByteDance added since. YES requires a new official 1260H update naming ByteDance or a parent/subsidiary. (a) The deadline is June 30, 2027, about 8.8 months away. (b) Status quo is NO. The statute only requires updates 'no less frequently than annually,' and the last update came about 17 months after the one before it, so a new list before the deadline is likely but not certain (roughly 55-65%). (c) NO scenario: the next update slips past June 2027, or it arrives but targets hardware, chip, EV and biotech firms like those on the Feinberg shortlist and in congressional letters (DeepSeek, Xiaomi, Gotion, etc.). ByteDance has appeared on none of these. Its TikTok issue was handled through the PAFACA/CFIUS divestiture, and the administration's TikTok deal and trade-truce posture lower the appetite to list it. (d) YES scenario: congressional anger over ByteDance's retained TikTok algorithm and 19.9% stake, shown in the Select Committee scrutiny, feeds into an H1 2027 update that names ByteDance or an AI subsidiary under a broad military-civil-fusion rationale. The subsidiary clause widens this path. The market sits at 16.5%. Given no shortlist mention, no congressional request and an uncertain update timing, I estimate roughly 60% × 15% ≈ 9-10%, a bit below the market.

Mean of 5 draws (0.13, 0.13, 0.12, 0.14, 0.14). The June 8, 2026 1260H update was an aggressive expansion (+65 entities including Alibaba, Baidu, BYD) yet deliberately omitted ByteDance, signaling the administration is applying a distinguishing factor tied to the January 2026 TikTok JV divestiture, which it has since treated as resolving national-security concerns (lifting the government-device ban). No DoD or congressional actor has been found explicitly pushing 1260H designation for ByteDance, and the Alibaba lawsuit raises the legal cost of further contestable additions. YES requires a subsequent update before June 2027 that reverses this stance; another update is plausible given the statutory annual cadence, but the historical cadence is irregular and the political incentive to protect the Trump-brokered TikTok deal points against designation. With no Kalshi direct price, I anchor on Polymarket's 16.5% and shade slightly lower given the specific evidence that ByteDance was passed over in the most expansive round.

Both forecasts converge near 11-12%, slightly below the 14% Polymarket proxy anchor, and the critique does not overturn this. The strongest evidence for No: ByteDance was passed over in the sweeping June 2026 update (65 new entities including Alibaba and Baidu), the completed TikTok divestiture defused the core rationale, no active DoD or congressional push exists, and the next scheduled update may fall at or after the June 30, 2027 close. The critique's valid points cut both ways — the timing-branch logic (update after close pushes YES toward near-zero) offsets the higher base-rate model mid (~20%) and the residual-products/off-cycle wildcards. I hold at 12% YES, preserving meaningful tail risk for a surprise Tencent/CATL-style addition given ByteDance's political salience, but weighting the narrow update window and defused rationale as dominant.

ByteDance's omission from the June 8, 2026 sweep that added 65 entities including directly comparable peers (Alibaba, Baidu, BYD) — plus its absence from every prior list and from the Dec 2025 congressional pressure letter — points to a structural rather than incidental exclusion, most plausibly the completed Jan 2026 TikTok US divestiture (19.9% residual stake) and DOJ's July 2026 PAFACA-compliance finding. The Polymarket anchor (~10.5%, declining, thin ~$15.7k volume) is a weak but directionally consistent signal, matching an independent base rate of ~9–15% for a scrutinized-but-unlisted firm over roughly one update cycle. The critique fairly notes upside tail risks — the withdrawn Feb 2026 draft's unknown contents, Warner/Markey pressure framing the divestiture as cosmetic, possible listing of a non-TikTok ByteDance Chinese subsidiary, and DoD potentially widening the net post-litigation — but these are offset by the litigation-driven incentive (Alibaba suit, Novogene dispute) for DoD to be more evidentiary and conservative. Given the thin anchor, I stay near it rather than shading far below, settling just under 10% and effectively splitting the two forecasts.

Will Donald Trump be the #1 searched per.rationale: Both forecasts converge near the 7% Polymarket anchor, and the core reasoning is sound: Google's spike-based methodology has excluded Trump in every non-campaign year (2017-2020, 2025), he is not on the 2026 ballot, and the US-hosted World Cup is already generating stronger competing spikes (Messi overtook him in July raw volume). The critique's strongest points — thin Polymarket liquidity and the possibility of a Trump-specific shock (health, impeachment, geopolitical crisis) as a sitting 80-year-old president — justify a small upward nudge above the pure anchor, but not a material departure, since even shocks around Trump historically haven't overcome the year-over-year spike hurdle for a chronically high-volume figure. The 2025 precedent (Mamdani topping People despite Trump's raw-volume dominance) is directly on point. Final call: 8% Yes, 92% No.

The structural case for No is strong: Google's Year in Search People list is spike/momentum-based, which penalizes a perpetually high-baseline figure like Trump, and he was absent entirely from the 2025 list despite being sitting president. His three #1 finishes (2016, 2020, 2024) all coincided with presidential elections; he is 0-for-7 in non-election years, and 2026 is a midterm year. The Polymarket anchor of 8.55% (declining) aligns with a ~10% base-rate model, though the thin $67k volume means it deserves only modest weight. The critique's point about Trump-specific tail events (health crisis at age 80, indictment, assassination attempt, contested midterms, 2028-adjacent shock) is fair and argues for sitting at or slightly above the market rather than below it, so I settle at 10% Yes.

Google's Year in Search People list ranks novel year-over-year search spikes, not sustained salience — Google itself said so when excluding Trump in 2017-2019. Trump has topped the US People list only in his own election-win years (2016, 2024) and was absent entirely in 2025 despite being sitting president, the strongest recent comparable. The ~20% raw base rate is misleading because it is fully concentrated in Trump-on-the-ballot years; in the ~8 non-Trump-election years the hit rate is zero, so a discount below 20% is justified even after granting the critique's point that midterms plus health/legal/assassination shock scenarios give a real but modest Yes path (and the 'not released by Mar 2027' clause mechanically favors No). The thin, declining Polymarket proxy at 9.15% carries limited weight on its own, but it coheres with the structural analysis, so I settle just at/above it at 10% rather than materially below.

Will the US acquire part of Greenland in.rationale: Mean of 5 draws (0.05, 0.05, 0.05, 0.04, 0.04). The Polymarket anchor for this exact contract is 5.25% with high liquidity and a stable, slightly declining trend; Kalshi analogs price even the 3-year horizon at only 22%, implying the 2026 window should be well below that. Nine months of 2026 have passed with no binding sovereignty or exclusive-jurisdiction instrument, Denmark and Greenland hold sovereignty as a firm red line, Trump disclaimed force on Jan 21, and the trilateral working group is trending toward expanded basing under the existing 1951/2004 framework, which would not qualify. The main residual risk is that a Q4 basing deal gets structured with US sovereign/exclusive-jurisdiction designation (an unconfirmed report says this was floated), or a resolution dispute over what counts, which keeps Yes above the floor. Historical base rate of failed US Greenland acquisition attempts further supports No.

No binding instrument transferring sovereignty or exclusive jurisdiction exists as of Aug 2026; talks remain within the 1951 defense treaty framework, Denmark and Greenland call sovereignty non-negotiable, 85% of Greenlanders oppose, and the required referendum plus Danish parliamentary approval have not begun, while all Greenland bills sit in committee. Both forecasters converged near 4.5-5%, and the critique fairly notes they discounted the market's 7% and underweighted two tails: a Guantanamo-style exclusive-jurisdiction basing arrangement (a materially lower bar than sovereignty) and unilateral/coercive executive action given Trump's repeated Jan/Jul/Aug escalation rhetoric. However, the near-term cross-market signals (0.3% for any new US territory by Jul 2026; 19-23% only over a full 3-year horizon) plus roughly four months remaining strongly favor No. I nudge slightly above the twin forecasts toward the anchor at ~5.5%, preserving a premium over the ~2%/yr base rate for persistent presidential intent and the exclusive-jurisdiction tail, while staying modestly below the salience-inflated 7% market price.

Will Trump speak to Mark Carney in Septe.rationale: Both forecasters landed at 0.58, and the critique's points largely cut in opposite directions: the unmet 'stop throwing shade' precondition and the deepening rift (Vance, Lutnick, mutual tariffs) argue for No, while the Sept 8 retaliation as a crisis-call trigger and UNGA high-level week (Carney planning to attend, Trump historically present, 2025 sideline-speaking precedent) argue for Yes. The Polymarket anchor is thin (~$23K) but is the only direct signal and has already cooled from 76% to 59.5% in response to the collapse, so it appears to have priced the rupture. With three-plus weeks remaining, a leader pair that spoke multiple times per month during the summer, and a natural late-September venue, the base rate favors some qualifying contact, but the severity of the suspension and lack of any scheduled bilateral justify a slight shade below the market. I hold at 0.58 Yes.

The only market anchor is a thin Polymarket proxy at 70.5% (~$19.6k volume, 5 data points, +13pt recent drift), which deserves partial but not full weight; the structural model blending an ~80% active-period base rate with a ~0-33% suspended-talks rate lands near 48%. A full month is a long window in a relationship that has repeatedly produced calls within days of tariff deadlines and retaliation announcements, and UNGA's late-September general debate is a genuine but unconfirmed catalyst (neither attendance nor a sidelines bilateral is verified). Against that, the late-August rupture — formal suspension of talks, 50% tariffs, and Carney's personal public rebuke — is qualitatively harsher than prior tense-but-functional stretches and could plausibly sustain a freeze through September, plus Carney faces domestic pressure to minimize engagement. I therefore sit modestly below both prior forecasts and well below the illiquid market, splitting the difference between the market signal and the suspended-state model at ~61%.

Will Xi Jinping purge Cai Qi in 2026?.rationale: Cai Qi was confirmed fully active and elevated (PSC #5, Secretariat first secretary, General Office director, new Central Party School president) through late August 2026 with no formal investigation against him personally, and no sitting PSC member has ever been purged mid-term under Xi (~0.3-1% loyalty-adjusted base rate). The best direct anchor is Polymarket's identical question at 7.2% (rising but thin at $47k), which likely carries the usual longshot/rumor premium of low-liquidity coup markets; the Li Qiang successor market at 9.5% is a weak comparator measuring a different event, so I give it little weight. The critique is right that 2026's unprecedented purge cadence (He Weidong, Zhang Youxia/Liu Zhenli, Ma Xingrui), associate-level probes into the 'Zhejiang network,' the October conclave, and the qualitatively distinct UK espionage vector make the historical zero-rate less binding than usual — so I do not discount as far below the market as both forecasters did. Settling at ~5.5% blends the near-zero structural base rate with a genuine, elevated tail risk over the remaining ~4-month window.

AI bubble burst in 2026?.rationale: Mean of 5 draws (0.07, 0.08, 0.07, 0.10, 0.11). Resolution requires ≥3 of 5 severe conditions (NVDA -50% from ATH, SOXX -40%, H100 ≤$1/hr for 5 days, lab bankruptcy/acquisition, major supplier -50%) and currently 0/5 are met: NVDA is only ~6-9% off its $235 ATH, SOXX ~20% off peak, H100 spot at $2.65/hr, and Nvidia's $105B OpenAI backstop plus a 94% Anthropic-IPO market signal no lab distress. Credit spreads (~2.7% HY OAS) and VIX (14-18) show no systemic stress. The historical base rate for a qualifying triple-condition crash is ~11-13% per full year, but only ~3.5 months remain and historical drawdowns of this magnitude typically unfold over many months, so the time-scaled probability is well below the annual rate. The Polymarket anchor at 12.3% likely reflects tail-risk premium; I shade below it to ~7% given the distance to thresholds and short remaining window.

The contract requires 3 of 6 extreme triggers within a single 90-day window before 2027-01-01, and none is close: NVDA is ~4% off its all-time high, H100 rentals are rising (~$2.5/hr vs a $1.00 trigger), and OpenAI/Anthropic are raising at record valuations with an IPO filing rather than showing distress; credit spreads and rates are benign. That makes a Yes require a fast, correlated crash — a genuine tail, not a linear extrapolation. I give modest weight to the red team's correlation/cascade point, the BofA Bubble Risk Indicator at 0.91, and the secondhand ~18% cross-market citation, which argues against shading below the Polymarket anchor; but the illustrative 20-45% simulation band was explicitly flagged as placeholder-quality and cannot override direct trigger-distance evidence. I therefore hold at the live market read of ~10% rather than discounting for time decay, ending slightly above Forecast 1 and level with Forecast 2.

The structural evidence strongly favors No: NVDA sits only ~8% below its all-time high (needing another ~45% fall), the closest trigger (SOXX at -20.8%) still needs 24pp more, TSM/ASML/AVGO are 40+pp away, H100 rentals are rising toward $2.50-7.48/hr rather than collapsing to $1, and OpenAI/Anthropic show zero distress (S-1 filed, $852B valuation, IPO plans). At most one condition (SMCI, ambiguous and partly recovered) is met, so three conditions require a violent correlated cascade within ~4 months. The devil's advocate is right that ρ≈0.8 correlated tail risk plus two >$1T selloffs and widening credit spreads mean a single catalytic shock could trip multiple triggers at once — this justifies pricing slightly above the Polymarket proxy of 12.7% rather than below it, and the Monte Carlo's 49-57% is not credible for a 4-month window from these starting distances. Cross-platform proxy mismatch adds uncertainty but not a clear directional bias. Final: 13% Yes.

Will the Republicans win the 2028 US Pre.rationale: Kalshi (41%) and Polymarket (40.5%) converge tightly on this exact question, giving a credible anchor even with thin Kalshi volume, since Polymarket's $1.12M turnover corroborates it. I shade modestly below the anchor because every independent fundamental points the same direction: post-1952 open-seat incumbent-party retention is ~12.5% (~27% since 1900), Trump approval sits at 34-38% with net approval near -20, the generic ballot is D+4 to D+6, and macro signals (PCE 4.5%, sentiment 55.2) are stagflationary. The critique is right that both forecasts under-weighted the base-rate gap, so I move a bit further toward No than the consensus 39%. But I do not blend heavily to 12-27%: over two years remain, no nominees are set, the Democratic field is fragmented (an AOC-type nominee is not clearly a general-election asset), Vance carries genuine VP/incumbency machinery, and small-n historical base rates deserve wide error bars. The reported 'Dem 59%' secondary print is discounted as stale or a different market instance, though it mildly reinforces the downward tilt.

Four venues (Kalshi 41%, Polymarket 40.5%, PredictIt/Covers ~42-45%) price the GOP near 40-42% with no cross-venue disagreement, which is the strongest available signal 2+ years out. The critique's two main pulls cut in opposite directions and largely cancel: the harsh open-seat base rate (12.5-20%, n=8, Laplace ~20%) and corroborating Dem-sweep/House signals argue for going below the market, while long-horizon mean reversion in approval and generic-ballot conditions argues for drifting back toward 50%. I give the base rate only modest weight because modern open-seat contests are far more competitive than the small mid-century sample implies (2000, 2016, 2024 were all near coin-flips) and because the market already embeds a substantial incumbent-party penalty relative to 50%. Third-party right-splitting risk and Vance's inheritance of a -20 net-approval administration are mild negatives; a unified GOP nominee and non-crisis macro are mild positives. I land at 40% YES, a hair under the Kalshi print reflecting the slight downward drift, with genuinely wide uncertainty.

Two independent order books agree tightly (Kalshi 42%, Polymarket 40.5%) with a stable 38-42% 90-day range, making the low-40s a credible anchor for a market with 2+ years of runway and no nominees. Directional evidence (Trump approval ~38-40%, independents ~34%, the Nov 2025 VA/NJ Democratic sweep, ~+4.5pt special-election overperformance, soft consumer sentiment) supports a modest shade below the anchor, but the 1/8 open-seat retention 'base rate' is an extremely small sample that conflates distinct eras and should not pull the estimate to 15-25%; markets already know these signals. The candidate-market/party-line 'tension' is not a real inconsistency — fast GOP consolidation says nothing about general-election strength — and the PredictIt figures sum above 100%, so they are non-normalized and uninformative. Counterweights (unemployment easing 4.4%→4.1%, modest GDP growth, no recession, midterm-backlash mean reversion after 2026) cut against extrapolating the current environment linearly to 2028. I settle at 40% Yes / 60% No, essentially at the market with a slight anti-incumbent-party tilt.

Will OpenAI have a #1 AI model by Decemb.rationale: Mean of 5 draws (0.28, 0.25, 0.26, 0.28, 0.28). The resolution source (Sep 13, 2026) shows Anthropic's claude-fable-5 at #1 with OpenAI's best model at rank 18, 23 Elo behind, and the Polymarket sibling anchor sits at 27.5% YES on a downtrend. Offsetting factors are that ties (overlapping CIs) count as YES, the top tier is clustered within noise, the crown has changed hands ~19 times in 41 months, OpenAI historically held #1 ~37% of months, and GPT-6 Astra (Sep 3) has not yet clearly registered on the board and could climb. With ~3.5 months left and a multi-way race where Google and Anthropic are at least as likely to hold #1 at the snapshot, a probability near the market anchor is appropriate, nudged slightly for OpenAI's release cadence and the tie rule.

OpenAI is not currently #1 on LMArena (Anthropic's Claude Fable 5/5.1 or Opus 5 leads most trackers, xAI on one), and GPT-6 Astra looks flat on adjacent indices, so the default is No. The critique's stronger points—that style-control-off Arena rankings have historically favored OpenAI's chat-tuned models relative to intelligence indices, that Astra remains unscored, that ~2 more leadership turnovers are plausible before Dec 31, and that normalized sibling markets imply ~40%—justify a modest nudge above the 30.5% Polymarket anchor and the ~32-33% base rate. Offsetting this, Anthropic's rapid cadence and a possible Gemini 3.5 Pro/4 release crowd OpenAI's path to the raw #1 rank (no ties in practice). I settle at 34% Yes, slightly above both forecasters but well short of the market-implied 40%.

OpenAI must reverse, not merely persist: GPT-5.6 Sol sits #3 at ~1514, roughly 11 Elo behind Claude Fable 5 (1525) with Claude Opus 5 (1522) in between, and Anthropic just refreshed its lineup in July 2026 while OpenAI's 'Astra'/GPT-6 has no confirmed date. The critique is right that the 'still #1' persistence base rate is the wrong frame — climbing from #3 in ~4 months is harder than holding — and that methodology volatility is symmetric, both of which argue for a modest shave below the anchor. Partly offsetting: the tie-counts-as-Yes criterion within a ~20-Elo cluster, LMArena re-baselining precedent, and a genuine (if unconfirmed) chance of a December OpenAI frontier launch given the ~11-month GPT-5→GPT-5.6 cadence. The Polymarket anchor at 28% is thin ($24k) but is the only real market signal and has been drifting mildly down. Net: 27% Yes, essentially at the anchor with a slight downward tilt for the reversal asymmetry.

The Polymarket print on this identical ticker (34% YES, uptrending) sits close to the ~30-32% historical share of time OpenAI has held LMArena's text #1, and the current snapshot is clearly unfavorable (Claude Fable 5 at ~1508-1525 while GPT-5.6 Sol reportedly sits well back). Both forecasters converged near the anchor; the critique's strongest points — the 'tie counts as YES' rule, common CI-overlapping top clusters, and roughly 2-3 more OpenAI releases before Dec 31 against a slipping Gemini 3.5 Pro — justify nudging slightly above the raw base rate, but not far, since OpenAI is not currently in the top cluster on this specific leaderboard. Methodology re-baseline risk and cross-leaderboard divergence (LLM Stats favors OpenAI) widen variance symmetrically rather than shifting the mean much, since the resolution source is fixed to LMArena where Anthropic currently dominates. I land at 36% YES, marginally above the market anchor to credit tie-resolution generosity and OpenAI's fast cadence.

Will the highest score achieved by an Op.rationale: The governing agi.safe.ai/Scale board shows OpenAI's confirmed best at 44.32% (GPT-5.4 Pro, Mar 2026), ~10.7 points short, and OpenAI is not even the overall leader (Gemini 3.1 Pro, 46.44%). The bullish case rests on unverified third-party figures (GPT-5.6 'Sol' ~49.5%) and on Astra, which as of Aug 2026 has no branding decision, no release, and no published HLE score — a genuine catalyst but far from assured to be benchmarked on the official board before Dec 31. The 55%+ scores circulating belong to Anthropic models, which is evidence of ecosystem progress but not of OpenAI-specific attainment, and OpenAI's own increment pace (44.3→~49.5 over four months, ~1.3 pts/mo) implies roughly landing near, not comfortably above, 55% by year-end. Adding official-verification/lag friction, I sit slightly below the noisy, thin-volume Polymarket proxy of 50.5% rather than above it, unlike both forecasters.

OpenAI's documented high-water mark is 49.5% (GPT-5.6 Sol, Aug 2026), leaving a 5.5-point gap with ~4.5 months and one announced-but-unreleased major model (Astra) remaining. The critique's deceleration argument is partly self-refuting: OpenAI moved from 43.1% (Apr) to 49.5% (Jul) on the tracked convention, a ~6.4-point gain in three months, so a further 5.5 points by year-end is well within recent pace if Astra ships on time — but Astra having no announced date is the key downside risk, and a slip into 2027 alone likely resolves No. Convention ambiguity (tool-augmented GPT-5.5 already at 52.2%) plus competitive pressure from Anthropic's 55.5% both tilt bullish and offset the thin-market discount on the 49.5% Polymarket anchor. I land marginally below the anchor at 0.47, reflecting that the trend model's lower blended range (35-45%) and the binary dependence on a single unscheduled release justify a modest lean toward No.

Will the highest score achieved by an An.rationale: Mean of 5 draws (0.30, 0.29, 0.30, 0.34, 0.34). The identical Polymarket question sits at ~33.5% YES and has fallen 31.5 points over 30 days, reflecting a plateau in Claude scores (Opus 4.8 at 57.9% w/tools → Fable 5.1 at 59.1% w/tools, only +1.2pts per cycle). Critically, the resolution source (agi.safe.ai / Scale's official leaderboard) shows Fable 5.1 at just 46.5% and the overall leader GPT-6 Astra at 54.8% — no model is within striking distance of 60% on the official methodology, and official figures persistently lag lab self-reports by 5-15 points. A Yes requires either a large jump from a late-2026 Claude release (plausible given Anthropic's cadence) or the leaderboard adopting tool-augmented scoring, both uncertain within ~3 months. I lean slightly below the market anchor given the resolution-source gap and the Monte Carlo central estimate of ~30-36%.

The named resolution source (agi.safe.ai/Scale AI) currently shows the best Claude entry at ~36–40%, roughly 20+ points short of the 60% threshold, while the frontier-wide official no-tools SOTA is only ~47% and has advanced ~10 points in 9 months — making a Claude leap to 60%+ on the official board within 2026 a genuine outlier scenario. Anthropic's self-reported Opus 5 numbers (56.3% no-tools / 64.7% with tools) already clear the bar, but independent replication (~53%) and the documented vendor-to-leaderboard discount pattern (36.2% listed vs. 64.7% claimed) suggest listing Opus 5 would likely still land short of 60%. The main YES pathways are therefore (a) resolution being adjudicated on self-reported/aggregator figures rather than the official leaderboard, or (b) a further generation (Opus 6-class) landing and being listed above 60% before year-end — each plausible but not dominant. The thin, volatile Polymarket price (58.5%, $33K volume, 17–65% range) most likely reflects conflation of self-reported with-tools claims with the actual resolution source, so I discount it substantially toward the leaderboard-anchored Monte Carlo range (25–36%), landing at ~0.33 Yes — below both prior forecasts, per the critique's stronger case.

The named resolution source (agi.safe.ai / Scale AI) is the binding constraint: as of August 2026 it still lists claude-opus-4-7 at 36.2% no-tools, with the overall official frontier only ~46-47%, and it has consistently lagged and undercut self-reported figures by 15-20pp. Applying that observed discount to Opus 5's self-reported 56.3% implies an eventual official score in the high-30s/low-40s, not ≥60%, and the with-tools 64.7% figure is likely a red herring since the official board reports closed-book/no-tools numbers. A YES therefore requires a compound conditional — a new (or existing) Claude scoring ≥60% under the stricter official protocol AND Scale AI posting it before Dec 31 — against a backdrop of decelerating, non-monotonic benchmark progress. I weight the mechanistic trend/lag evidence (8-15%) more heavily than the thin, highly volatile Polymarket 60% anchor, but keep meaningful upside for definitional looseness (headline/third-party scores being accepted) and a possible Q4 flagship, landing at 0.33 — below both forecasters and well below the market.

Both forecasters essentially anchored to Polymarket's 50.5% and nudged up, without independently pricing the conjunction required for Yes: the official agi.safe.ai leaderboard must (a) actually update with a Claude entry before Dec 31 and (b) display an accuracy of ≥60%. The strongest documented facts push the other way: the official snapshot still shows only Opus 4.7 at ~36.2% with a confirmed multi-month lag, the primary leaderboard column is no-tools where Anthropic's own best self-report is 56.3% (short of 60%), and third-party recomputes have historically come in below Anthropic's self-serving framing (Opus 4.6: 40.0% recompute vs 'leads all frontier models' claim), with grader revisions an additional downside risk. Paths to Yes remain real — a with-tools column at 64.7%, a post-Opus-5 release (Fable/Mythos variants), and a genuinely fast-moving benchmark — which is why I don't go far below the market. Scenario weighting (roughly 55-65% chance of a timely official Claude update × ~55-65% chance that update reads ≥60%, plus a modest with-tools/wildcard boost) lands just under the coin-flip anchor.

NATO downs another Russian drone by Sept.rationale: The empirical tempo is the strongest evidence: at least five to six distinct NATO shoot-down episodes between June 8 and Aug 16, 2026 (~0.5/week), with no ceasefire, open-ended Eastern Sentry, centralized post-Ankara engagement authority, and Romania logging 42+ scrambles in 2026. A naive Poisson over a ~2.5-3 week window gives ~70-78%, well above the thin Polymarket proxy at 42.5% (3 data points, ~$24K volume, no Kalshi anchor retrieved). I discount the raw Poisson for three reasons the critique correctly raises: mean-reversion risk from an unusually hot summer tempo, the fact that many incursions (Aug 20 Tulcea, Jul 30 Poland debris) are tracked or crash without engagement, and confirmation/resolution-lag risk near the deadline. Balancing a heavily-weighted base rate against a lightly-weighted, declining but unreliable market proxy lands me at ~62% YES, between the two forecasts but closer to the base-rate view, with acknowledged wide uncertainty given the missing Kalshi anchor.

Anthropic currently holds #1 on arena.ai Text Arena Overall per two trackers, has just shipped its strongest models (Fable 5.1/Mythos 5.1), and occupies multiple top slots (Opus 4.8 and 4.7), which raises the odds that some Anthropic model sits at #1 on the Oct 31 snapshot even if individual rankings shuffle. However, the lead is under 50 Elo ('coin flip' range), GPT-6 Astra is already live and could climb as votes accumulate, a Gemini 4 launch is rumored for October explicitly to retake the top, and arena rankings have historically flipped with nearly every major lab release. The 86.5% Polymarket price is a thin-market proxy with a suspicious +12% weekly jump, so I weight it less than a liquid Kalshi quote would warrant. The exact-contract Polymarket price (85.5% YES, rising, sibling markets structurally coherent) is the single most informative signal and should be the primary anchor; the critique correctly notes Forecast 1's discount rests on an unsupported reference-class claim that the brief explicitly contradicts (Anthropic repeatedly held #1 in 2026). Corroborating evidence — Anthropic models at or near LMArena #1 in Aug 2026 plus Opus 5 leading the independent Artificial Analysis index — supports the market's lean, and Anthropic's own dense release cadence means it is likely to be a leapfrogger rather than only a leapfrog victim. Offsetting factors justify a modest discount below 85.5%: the evidence is ~2 months stale, the top cluster is within 15-30 ELO (noise-sensitive), 2-4 leapfrog cycles from OpenAI/Google/xAI could occur before Oct 31, thin $15K liquidity limits price reliability, and the 'unavailable/Other' branch breaks toward No. Netting these, I land near 0.77 — above Forecast 1's overly aggressive discount and close to but slightly above Forecast 2.

Will Alysa Liu be the #1 searched athlet.rationale: The only live anchor is a thin (~$17.5K) Polymarket quote at 17.5% that has risen sharply post-Olympics, which suggests retail momentum bias rather than calibrated pricing; a synthetic multi-candidate view implies closer to 7-9%, so the truth likely sits between, modestly below the market. Structurally, no figure skater has ever topped Google's Global Athletes list (best: Hanyu #6 in 2022), and winners skew to soccer, boxing, tennis and cricket — sports with far larger worldwide audiences than U.S. figure skating. The critique correctly notes 2022's winner was Djokovic despite a World Cup, so the World Cup headwind is weaker than framed, but it also correctly notes the crucial gap between 'top-5' (plausible for Liu, as U.S.-centric surges like Sanders/Hurts have charted) and '#1' (a much bigger leap requiring global, not just American, search dominance). Liu's Instagram explosion and pop-culture crossover are real but demonstrably U.S.-concentrated, which fits the U.S. list better than the global one. Netting these, I settle a touch below both forecasts at 13% Yes.

Will Google be the third-best AI lab at.rationale: Both forecasts converge on the Polymarket anchor (16.5% YES) for the identical contract, and the critique does not surface evidence that would justify moving materially in either direction: thin liquidity and tiebreak randomness argue for slightly more uncertainty, while the July precedent (Google's third-place share collapsing toward ~0%) and the recent 7-day collapse from 65.5% argue the market may still be generous to Yes. Fundamentals favor No: Anthropic is a clear #1, OpenAI's GPT-5.5 Pro sits in the same ~1500-1510 cluster as Gemini 3.1 Pro, Google has shipped only Flash-tier updates with no confirmed flagship before Sept 30, and Meta adds a possible additional podium competitor. 'Exactly 3rd' is a narrow target in a near-tied 3-4 lab cluster, and a surprise Gemini flagship could push Google to #2 (also No) or fail to accrue enough votes before the snapshot. I hold at 17% YES, essentially at the market with offsetting adjustments.

The critique's dedup point is the decisive correction: 'Lab Rank' collapses multiple models per lab, so Google's #9 model rank in the DataLearner snapshot (Anthropic at 1/2/3/5/6/7, Meta at 4/8) actually maps to roughly the #3 lab slot once duplicates are removed, while the swfte-style snapshot (Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI ahead) maps Google to ~#4.
